en: A person or thing that translates various forms of text.
Synonym of interpreter, a person or thing that immediately interprets direct speech.

en: To send or convey from one person, place or thing to another.

tutor.ety: From Middle English tutour, from Old French tuteur (French tuteur), from Latin tūtor (“a watcher, protector, guardian”), from tueor (“protect”); see tuition.

ex.ja: 家庭教師の先生は私が馬鹿なことをしたと叱った。

en: A rod or staff of office, e.g. of a verger.

To bend or incline; to tend downward; to slope.

verge.ety: Borrowed from Middle French verge (“rod or wand of office”), hence "scope, territory dominated", from Latin virga (“shoot, rod stick”), of unknown origin. Earliest attested sense in English is now-obsolete meaning "male member, penis" (c.1400). Modern sense is from the notion of 'within the verge' (1509, also as Anglo-Norman dedeinz la verge), i.e. "subject to the Lord High Steward's authority" (as symbolized by the rod of office), originally a 12-mile radius round the royal court, which sense shifted to "the outermost edge of an expanse or area." en: To slope or incline (something); to slant.
To be at an angle.

tilt.ety:
From Middle English tilte, from Old English *tyltan, *tieltan (“to be unsteady”), related to the adjective tealt (“unsteady”), from Proto-West Germanic *talt, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *del-, *dul- (“to shake, hesitate”), see also Dutch touteren (“to tremble”), North Frisian talt, tolt (“unstable, shaky”). The soft fruit borne by this shrub, formed of a black (when ripe) cluster of drupelets.

A line segment between two points of a curve.
To write chords for.
To accord; to harmonize together.

Pertaining to the body (the thorax and abdomen), as distinguished from the head, limbs and wings, etc.
A non-commissioned officer army rank with NATO code OR-4. The rank below a sergeant but above a lance corporal and private.
A non-commissioned officer rank in the police force, below a sergeant but above a private or patrolman.

corporal.ety: From Middle English corporal, corporall, corporel, corporell, from Old French corporal (French corporel), from Latin corporālis, from Latin corpus (“body”); compare corporeal.

ex.ja: 世論の趨勢は体罰反対の方向である。

Historically, the wager of battle (judicial combat).
To engage in a battle.

duel.ety:
From Medieval Latin duellum (“fight between two men, duel”), itself from Old Latin duellum (“war, fight”), which survived in Classical Latin as a rare byform of bellum and was later reinterpreted as “duel” by unetymological association with duo (“two”).

An art or craft object made by hand.

ex.en: All of them were handmade things.
ex.ja: それは全て手作りのものだった。

ex.ja: おばあちゃんの手作り弁当は、私の胃袋を支えてくれている。

ex.en: Handmade goods are very expensive nowadays.

en: The act of something happening; occurrence.
The extent or the relative frequency of something happening.

incidence.ety: From Middle French incidence, from Medieval Latin incidentia (“a falling upon”), from Latin incidens, present participle of incidere (“to fall upon”), from in (“on”) + cadere (“to fall”).

en: Feeling or atmosphere of closeness and openness towards someone else, often but not necessarily involving sexuality.
Intimate relationship.

ex.en: Their intimacy grew with the years.

A young rabbit, rat, hedgehog, squirrel, fox, beaver, badger, etc.
To give birth to kittens.

Seemingly from, and usually explained as being from, unattested Anglo-Norman *kitoun, *ketun (compare Old French chitoun, cheton, chaton (“kitten”), diminutive of cat, chat (“cat”)); whence Modern French chaton (“kitten”). Similar words of Germanic origin may have reinforced this word; compare English kitling (“kit, kitten”), Low German Kitten (“kitten”), Icelandic kettlingur (“kitten”), Middle English chitte ("whelp, pup", see chit). ex.ja: 小猫がテーブルの下でミルクを飲んでいた。

ex.en: The kitten couldn't get down from the tree.
ex.ja: 子猫は木から降りられなかった。

ex.en: I'll give these kittens to whoever likes cats.
ex.ja: 私はこの小猫を猫の好きな人には誰にでもあげます。

To move with a lever.
To use, operate or move (something) like a lever (physically).

lever.ety: From Middle English lever, levore, levour, from Old French leveor, leveur (“a lifter, lever (also Old French and French levier)”), from Latin levātor (“a lifter”), from levō (“to raise”). Doublet of levator.

ex.en: Please push up the lever.
ex.ja: レバーを押しあげて下さい。

ex.en: They lifted the rock by means of a lever.
ex.ja: 彼らはその岩をてこで持ち上げた。

ex.en: You can adjust the seat height by moving the adjustment lever up.
ex.ja: 調節レバーを上に上げると座面の高さを調節できます。

en: That which has mutated, with one or more new characteristics from a mutation.
Someone or something that seems strange, abnormal, or bizarre.
Of, relating to, undergoing (i.e. mutating), or resulting from change or mutation; that has undergone mutation.
Strange, abnormal, or bizarre.

mutant.ety: From Latin mūtāns, present participle of mūtō. By surface analysis, muta- + -ant.

en: The collection of myths of a people, concerning the origin of the people, history, deities, ancestors and heroes.
A similar body of myths concerning an event, person or institution.

mythology.ety: First attested as Middle English in 1412. From Middle French mythologie, from Latin mȳthologia, from Ancient Greek μυθολογία (muthología, “legend”) μυθολογέω (muthologéō, “to tell tales”), from μυθολόγος (muthológos, “legend”), from μῦθος (mûthos, “story”) + λέγω (légō, “to say”). By surface analysis, myth + -ology or mytho- + -logy.

ex.en: In Greek mythology, Ares was the god of war.
ex.ja: ギリシャ神話では、アレスは戦争の神でした。

ex.en: The story of a great flood is very common in world mythology.
ex.ja: 世界神話の中でも、大洪水の話はとても有名だ。

ex.en: For some reason economic booms have names taken from Japanese mythology given to them.
ex.ja: なぜか、景気の良いときには日本の神話にちなんだ名前が付けられています。

en: The chemical element (symbol Ne) with an atomic number of 10. The second of the noble gases, it is a colourless, odorless inert gas.
A form or sample of the element.
That resembles a neon light; extremely bright; fluorescent

Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek νέον (néon), neuter of νέος (néos, “new”), from Proto-Hellenic *newos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos. By surface analysis, neo- + -on (suffix used in all noble gases).

ex.en: Tom's fursona is a fox named Neon.
ex.ja: トムのファーソナはネオンという名前のキツネだよ。

ex.en: The neon sign shone as if to invite us.
ex.ja: 私たちを招くようにネオンサインが輝いていた。

en: Of, related to, located in, or from the northeast.

northeastern.ety: From Middle English norþesterne, from Old English norþēasterne, equivalent to north + eastern.

en: A member of a Christian religious community of women who live by certain vows and usually wear a habit, (Roman Catholicism, specifically)…
A member of a similar female community in other confessions.

nun.ety: From Middle English nonne, nunne, from Old English nunne (“nun”), from Late Latin nonna (“nun, tutor”), originally (along with masculine form nonnus (“man”)) a term of address for elderly persons, perhaps from children's speech, reminiscent of nana, like papa etc. Doublet of nonna.

ex.en: The nun prayed and crossed herself.
ex.ja: 尼僧はお祈りをして十字を切った。

ex.en: When she became a nun, she took the name Sister Teresa.
ex.ja: 修道女になったとき、シスター・テレサの名を受けた。

ex.en: She led a group of nuns called the Missionaries of Charity.
ex.ja: 彼女は慈善伝導団と呼ばれる修道女達の集団を指導していた。

an orthopedic structure or a footlike part.

To operate a bicycle.
Of or relating to the foot.

ex.en: Press the brake pedal to turn on your brake lights.
ex.ja: ブレーキペダルを押して、ブレーキライトをつけてみてください。

en: Any destructive insect that attacks crops or livestock; an agricultural pest.
An annoying person, a nuisance.

pest.ety: In the 16th century in the sense of "pestilence" and specifically bubonic plague from Middle French peste (“pestilence”) (whence French peste). The other meanings are recorded soon after. Ultimately from Latin pestis.

ex.ja: ベタベタするんじゃねえよっ！鬱陶しい！

en: A large post, often used as supporting architecture.
Something resembling such a structure.
To provide with pillars or added strength as if from pillars.

pillar.ety: From Middle English piler, from Old French pilier, from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin *pilāre (“a pillar”), from Latin pila (“a pillar, pier, mole”). Displaced native Old English sweor (“pillar, column”) and Old English stapol.

ex.ja: 柱にナイフが突き刺さっていた。

ex.en: These pillars are made of stone.
ex.ja: これは石柱である。

ex.en: These pillars support the stage.
ex.ja: これらの柱が舞台を支えています。

en: Seemingly or apparently valid, likely, or acceptable; conceivably true or likely.
Obtaining approbation; specifically pleasing; apparently right; specious.

plausible.ety: From Latin plausibilis (“deserving applause, praiseworthy, acceptable, pleasing”), from the participle stem of plaudere (“to applaud”).

ex.en: Your explanation sounds plausible, but it just doesn't hold water.
ex.ja: 君の説明はもっともらしいが、筋がちっとも通ってない。

ex.en: You're spitting out plausible lies.
ex.ja: もっともらしい嘘をつきやがって。

ex.en: A more plausible proposal is the one Leech presented in conjunction with Emmet's theory.
ex.ja: リーチがエメット理論との関連で提供した提案のほうがより妥当なものである。

A material consisting of such polymer molecules.

polymer.ety: From poly- + -mer, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) + μέρος (méros, “part”). Coined by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1833, though his definition was quite different from the modern one.

The amount of water precipitated in any form.

precipitation.ety: From Middle French précipitation, from Latin praecipitātiō, praecipitātiōnem. By surface analysis, precipitate + -ion.

en: A period of 40 days, particularly
The 40-day period during which a widow is entitled to remain in her deceased husband's home while any dower is collected and returned.
To place into isolation to prevent the spread of any contagious disease.
To enter or stay in quarantine, particularly to self-quarantine to avoid an epidemic disease.

quarantine.ety:
From Medieval Latin quarentena and quarentīna (“40-day period, Lent”) via Middle English quarentine, Norman quarenteine, French quarenteine, and Italian quarantina, via proposed Late Latin *quaranta + -ēna (forming distributive adjectives), from Latin quadrāgintā (“four tens, 40”).
In reference to French politics, calque of French quarantaine after edicts of Louis IX. In reference to a severance of political relations, popularized by the Roosevelt administration's 1937 approach to the Axis powers and the later Kennedy administration's 1962 approach to Cuba during the missile crisis.

ex.en: People returning from Spain are required to self-quarantine for 14 days.
ex.ja: スペインから帰国する人全員に14日間の自主隔離を義務付けた。

ex.en: The hospital quarantined the infected patients to avoid cross infection.
ex.ja: 病院は院内感染を防ぐため、感染患者を隔離した。

en: A question, an inquiry (US), an enquiry (UK).
A question mark.
To ask a question.
To ask, inquire.

query.ety: An anglicisation of quere, an obsolete variant form of Latin quaere, second-person singular present active imperative of quaerō (“seek, look for; ask”); perhaps suffixed with -y (“abstract noun”). Cognate with French quérir, Italian chiedere, Portuguese querer, Romanian cere, and Spanish querer. Compare question.

ex.en: The saleswoman queried as she wrapped the gloves.
ex.ja: 美人店員は手袋を袋に包みながら尋ねた。

en: Something that restrains, ties, fastens or secures.
Control or caution; reserve.

restraint.ety: From Middle English restreynte, from Old French restreinte; more at restrain.

ex.en: She was angry, but she spoke with restraint.
ex.ja: 彼女は怒っていたが、それをおさえて話をした。

ex.en: He refused to exercise self-restraint.
ex.ja: 彼は自粛の波に乗らなかった。

ex.en: Institutionally, a major restraint is the copyright problem.

A lack of cohesion; a state of conflict, incompatibility, or emotional distance.
To form a rift; to split open.
To cleave; to rive; to split.

rift.ety: From Middle English rift, of North Germanic origin; akin to Danish rift, Norwegian Bokmål rift (“breach”), Old Norse rífa (“to tear”). More at rive.

Cloth of a scarlet color.
Of a bright red colour.
Sinful or whorish.
To dye or tinge (something) with scarlet.

scarlet.ety: From Middle English scarlet, scarlat, borrowed from Old French escarlate (“a type of cloth”), from Medieval Latin scarlātum (“scarlet cloth”), of uncertain origin. This was long thought to derive from Classical Persian سقرلات (saqirlāt, “a warm woollen cloth”), but the Persian word (first attested in the 1290s) is now thought to be from Arabic سِقِلَّات (siqillāt), denoting very expensive, luxury silks dyed scarlet-red using the exceptionally expensive dye, first attested around the ninth century. en: A pipe or channel, or system of pipes or channels, used to remove human waste and to provide drainage.
To provide (a place) with a system of sewers.

sewer.ety: From Middle English sewer, seuer, from Anglo-Norman sewere (“water-course”), from Old French sewiere (“overflow channel for a fishpond”), from Vulgar Latin *exaquāria (“drain for carrying water off”), from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + aquāria (“of or pertaining to waters”) or from a root *exaquāre.
